On Saturday, the seventeenth of May two thousand and thirty-six, Margarete Hoffmann turned a hundred. She woke up that morning at six, as always, and the first thing she saw when she opened her eyes was a letter on her bedside table, with a golden eagle on it, from the Federal President, who, as it said in very fine bureaucratic German, conveyed to her “on the occasion of the completion of her hundredth year of life the warmest congratulations”. Grete had the night nurse read it to her, twice, and then said: “How nice. He doesn't even know me.” Then she asked for her hat, the small black one with the feather, and her lipstick, which she had worn in the same colour since the day of her first concert, a dark red that, as she claimed, could only be found in a single chemist's in Berlin.

The party was to take place at three in the afternoon in the big hall of the care home, the same hall in which Grete, three years ago, after her pneumonia, had played the Brahms sonata to the end, the same hall in which Friedrich's memorial service had been held. Frau Petersen had prepared everything, with a meticulousness that reminded Ludwig of the old BVB: rows of chairs, a lectern for the speakers, flowers in vases on every windowsill, a table of cakes almost as long as the hall. And at the front, where the old grand piano at which Grete had taught for so many years usually stood, there was something else, something nobody was expecting, covered with a white cloth, like a monument before its unveiling.

More people came than the hall could hold. Everyone from Kastanienallee came, of course, and all the residents of the care home who could still walk or be wheeled in. Grete's former pupils came, forty, fifty people between twenty and eighty, some from Hamburg, from Cologne, one even from New York, where, as he told Ludwig, he had been playing the piano in the Metropolitan Opera orchestra for thirty years. He had learnt with Grete as a child, in the seventies, and she, as he put it, “once shouted at me so loudly that I decided to become a pianist, just to prove to her that I could”. And Frau Winter from the publishing house came, with a parcel under her arm that she held like a treasure.

Hotte came in his best tram driver's cap, freshly brushed, and sat down, without asking, in the front row, right next to the seat reserved for Grete. When Frau Petersen politely asked him to sit further back, he just said: “I'm ninety-one. Next to a hundred-year-old, I'm the youngest in the room. I'm stayin'.” Frau Petersen let him be. Dr Vogt came straight from the night shift, with dark circles under his eyes and a single white rose. Ayşe Yilmaz had baked baklava for three nights, so much that two trays were left over, which she shared out among the staff in the evening. And Leo came in uniform, after the morning shift, with a framed drawing that a little boy in a red jacket had given him and which, as he explained to Grete, he had actually wanted to hang in his cab, but today he was lending it to her, because it was about people who had been there on time.

Grete was wheeled into the hall at three by Mara, in her wheelchair, with the black hat and the dark red lipstick, and when she came in, everyone stood up, and there was no applause but something more beautiful: silence. A hundred, two hundred people stood in a hall and were silent, and in that silence all you could hear were the wheels of the chair on the parquet and the soft ticking of a clock on the wall. Grete looked around, slowly, with her clear, ironic gaze, and then said, loudly enough to be heard in the back row: “Well. You look as if somebody had died. Sit down. I'm still alive.” And the whole hall laughed, and the silence was over, and the party began.

Ludwig gave his speech first. He had practised it for three days with Lena, shortened it, rewritten it, cut the stiff beginning and replaced it with a memory, and in the end it was exactly ninety seconds long. He stood at the lectern, leaning on his stick, and spoke without notes. He told how Grete had first heard him play the guitar ten years ago, when she was ninety and he was seventy-seven, in the courtyard on Kastanienallee, when he was playing the guitar for the first time since Ingrid's death, and Grete had shouted from the window that he played “like a tram driver, that is, always in the same rhythm, no matter what happens along the route”. “She was right,” said Ludwig. “But she listened to me anyway. And the next day she showed me how to brake. In music too.”

“Without you,” said Ludwig, and now he was looking only at Grete, “there would have been much less playing in this house and on our street. Much less singing. Much less laughter. We owe you the piano in this hall, the music on Kastanienallee and a girl who can play Brahms on a kitchen table, without a single sound, and whom you can hear all the same.” He paused. “Please raise your glasses,” he said. “To Grete. To a hundred years. And to the girl at the table.” Two hundred glasses were raised, with champagne, with juice, with water, and two hundred voices said: “To Grete!” And Grete, in the front row, didn't raise her glass, because her hand was shaking too much. But she raised her chin. And that, Mara said later, was more.

Then Frau Winter came to the lectern. She opened the parcel, very slowly, and took out a book. It was thin, only a hundred and twenty pages, bound in dark red cloth, exactly the colour of Grete's lipstick, and on the cover there was a photograph: an old kitchen table with a keyboard drawn on it in chalk, two octaves, black and white. It was Elif's table. Andrei had photographed it in February, before the chalk was wiped off. Above it, in simple gold letters, it said: “Margarete Hoffmann. Das Mädchen am Tisch. Memories. Written by Elif Yilmaz.” Frau Winter placed the book in Grete's hands, carefully, and held her hands so that the book wouldn't fall. “The first print run,” she said. “Five hundred copies. Sold out since yesterday. The second is being printed now.”

Grete looked at the book for a long time. She ran her finger over the cover, over the chalk keys in the photograph, as if she could play them. Then she opened it, with Frau Winter's help, at the first page, and read the dedication she had dictated herself, in March, on one of the bad days, when she could hardly speak any more. It just said: “For Herr Wendland, who played in the dark. For my mother, who was silent. And for Elif, who listened.” Grete closed the book. She said nothing. She searched the hall with her eyes until she found Elif, who was sitting in the second row, between her mother and Ludwig, and had blushed to the roots of her hair. Grete nodded to her. Just once. It was, as Elif later wrote in her diary, the greatest praise she had ever received.

Then the white cloth at the front of the hall was pulled away. Underneath stood the Yilmaz family's kitchen table, the real one, from the second-floor flat at number thirty-three, carried across half of Berlin that morning by Andrei and Leo. On its top, freshly drawn in new chalk, was a keyboard. And beside it, in its usual place, stood the old grand piano, open. Elif stood up, went to the front, sat down first at the table and put her hands on the wood. She played. Without a sound. The beginning of Brahms's Intermezzo in A major, opus 118, the piece Herr Wendland had played in the cellar in February nineteen forty-four. Two hundred people were watching an eleven-year-old girl playing on a kitchen table, and nobody said a word, and some, Hotte said later, would have sworn they heard the music.

After eight bars, Elif stood up, took the three steps from the table to the piano, sat down and played on. With sound. Exactly at the point where she had stopped on the table. The first notes fell into the silence of the hall like drops into a lake, and Grete, in the front row, closed her eyes, as she always did when she listened to music. Elif didn't play perfectly. In the difficult passage in the middle she hesitated, and once she hit a wrong key. But she played the way Grete had taught her, with Herr Wendland's metronome, which she had brought along and which stood on the piano, switched off, just as a witness. She played the piece to the end. And when the last note died away, the hall was so quiet that you could hear the ticking of the clock on the wall again.

Grete opened her eyes. She beckoned Mara over, whispered something in her ear, and Mara pushed the wheelchair forward, right up to the piano. Elif wanted to stand up, but Grete shook her head. “Stay seated,” she said. “Move over a bit.” Elif moved over. And Grete, who hadn't played for two years because her hands shook too much, raised her right hand, slowly, with great effort, and placed it on the keys, next to Elif's hands. She played just one line. The top voice of the last four bars, with one finger, trembling, note by note, while Elif played the accompaniment underneath, softly, carefully, the way you support someone climbing a staircase. Four hands. Two eleven-year-old hands and one hundred-year-old one. Then it was over. Grete took her hand off the keys and laid it in her lap.

This time there was applause. It went on for so long that Frau Petersen finally had to come to the lectern and ask for quiet, because otherwise the cakes would get warm, which in the case of the cream gateau, as she said, “could not be justified”. Grete laughed. She laughed the way Ludwig hadn't heard her laugh for months, loudly, a little hoarsely, with her head thrown back, so that the little black hat almost fell off. And when Ludwig, later that evening, after everyone had left, came to her room once more to tell her the promised ten seconds that hadn't been in his speech, she was already asleep. She was holding the dark red book in her arms. And on her face there was an expression Ludwig had seen only once before: on Ingrid, the evening she finished reading “Emil und die Detektive” for the last time. Content. Fulfilled. Not sad.

On the occasion of her hundredth birthday, the pianist Margarete Hoffmann was celebrated in Pankow on Saturday.
Her memoirs, “The Girl at the Table”, written by her eleven-year-old pupil Elif Yilmaz, had already sold out the day before the party.
The highlight of the afternoon was a Brahms intermezzo, played first without sound on a kitchen table and then on the piano.
The last bars were played by the guest of honour herself, with one finger. “You don't need more than that,” she said afterwards, “when someone is sitting next to you.”
